nameStory: Cannabis gets its name from the ancient Greek word 'kannabis,' which itself likely came from a Scythian or Thracian word meaning 'hemp.' The species name 'sativa' means 'cultivated' in Latin, reflecting humanity's long relationship with this plant as a crop for fiber, food, and medicine spanning thousands of years.
description: Cannabis is a tall, fast-growing annual herb that can reach 3-16 feet in height during a single growing season. It has distinctive palm-shaped leaves with serrated edges and develops either male flowers (small clusters) or female flowers (sticky, resinous buds) on separate plants. The plant has a strong, distinctive odor that becomes more pronounced as it matures, and its sturdy, hollow stems are covered in fine hairs.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive palmate leaves with 3-11 narrow, lance-shaped leaflets radiating from a central point like fingers on a hand. Leaflets have sharply serrated edges and feel slightly rough to the touch with visible veins.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Male plants produce small, pale green flowers in drooping clusters that release pollen. Female plants develop tight clusters of small, greenish flowers that become increasingly sticky and resinous with a strong, skunky aroma.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a single-stemmed, upright plant with opposite branching that becomes alternate higher up. Stems are hollow, ridged, and covered in fine white hairs that give them a slightly fuzzy texture.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Female plants produce small, hard, oval seeds (often called hemp hearts) that are grayish-brown with darker mottled patterns. Seeds have a smooth, slightly waxy feel and a mild, nutty taste.

habitat: In New England, cannabis is occasionally found as an escape from cultivation in disturbed soils, vacant lots, roadsides, and waste areas. It prefers well-drained, fertile soils in full sun and doesn't typically establish persistent wild populations due to New England's climate.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil temperatures warm. Young plants emerge with their characteristic three-leaflet seedling leaves before developing the classic palmate mature leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly through summer, developing full size and distinctive foliage. Male plants begin flowering in mid to late summer, while females start developing flower clusters.
seasonality.fall: Flowering peaks in early fall as day length shortens. Female plants become increasingly aromatic and resinous. Seeds mature and disperse before first frost kills the annual plants.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist through winter as dry, hollow stalks, but living plants cannot survive New England's freezing temperatures.

funFact: Cannabis plants are either entirely male or entirely female (dioecious), and you can actually tell them apart by smell - male plants have a milder, grassy scent while females develop that characteristic strong, musky aroma that can be detected from quite a distance!
confusionNotes: The distinctive palmate leaves make cannabis difficult to confuse with other plants, though some people mistake Japanese maple seedlings or Virginia creeper for young cannabis plants. Remember: cannabis leaves are serrated all the way to their tips and grow in opposite pairs, while Virginia creeper has smooth leaf margins and climbs, and Japanese maple seedlings have much more delicate, deeply lobed leaves.
contextualKnowledge: While cannabis has a complex legal status, it's important to know that hemp (low-THC cannabis) and marijuana (high-THC cannabis) are the same species - just different varieties bred for different purposes. Hemp has been legally grown in some New England states for industrial fiber and seeds, which explains some of the observation records.
compareHints: Cannabis is the only species in its genus found in New England. Within the Cannabaceae family, it's easily distinguished from its relatives like hackberries and elms by its distinctive palmate leaves and herbaceous annual growth habit, whereas other family members are typically woody trees or shrubs with simple, oval leaves.
